title: 贾生
author: 李商隐
intro: An emperor summons a brilliant exiled scholar and talks with him until midnight, leaning in eagerly — only to ask about ghosts and spirits, not about the people. A sharp four-line irony about wasted talent.
analysis: 贾谊是西汉初年的天才政治家，二十多岁就提出很多治国的主张，却被排挤，贬到长沙。几年后汉文帝把他召回，在宣室接见他。据《史记》记载，文帝问的是鬼神的事，贾谊讲得很好，文帝听得入神，半夜里不自觉地把座席往前移。这首诗前两句先扬：皇帝在宣室访求贤才，召回被贬的大臣，贾谊的才华无人能比。第三句一个“可怜”（可惜）一转，第四句点破：不问百姓的事，只问鬼神。前面越写皇帝重视人才，后面的讽刺就越尖锐，这种写法叫“先扬后抑”。诗人借汉代的故事，讽刺晚唐皇帝迷信求仙、不关心百姓，也抒发了自己怀才不遇的感慨。
analysisEn: Jia Yi (200–168 BC) was a young genius of the early Han dynasty who, in his twenties, proposed bold reforms — and was pushed out of court and sent to faraway Changsha. Years later Emperor Wen called him back and received him in the Xuanshi Hall. According to the historian Sima Qian, the emperor asked about ghosts and spirits; Jia Yi answered so well that the emperor, listening late into the night, kept moving his sitting mat closer without noticing. Li Shangyin tells this story in four lines. The first two praise: the emperor seeks talent, summons the exiled minister, and Jia Yi’s gifts are beyond compare. Line three turns on the word 可怜 (“what a pity”), and line four delivers the blow: he asked not about the common people, but about ghosts and gods. The more the opening builds up the emperor’s respect, the sharper the irony at the end — a technique called “raise first, then lower”. Through a Han story the poet criticises late Tang emperors who chased immortality potions and neglected their people, and also voices his own frustration as a talented man nobody used well.
background: Li Shangyin (c. 813–858) was one of the great poets of the late Tang, famous for dense, beautiful and often mysterious verse. Caught between two rival court factions, he spent most of his life in minor posts. Several late Tang emperors were obsessed with Daoist elixirs; Emperor Wuzong died in 846 after taking them.
pronunciation: 才调 cái diào（才气，不读 tiáo）；更 gèng；前席 qián xí。
version: 采用通行本，各本一致。故事出自《史记·屈原贾生列传》。

lines.py: xuān shì qiú xián fǎng zhú chén
lines.lit: In the Xuanshi Hall, seeking the worthy, he sought out the banished minister;
lines.en: Seeking wise men, the emperor called the exile back to his hall;

lines.py: jiǎ shēng cái diào gèng wú lún
lines.lit: Master Jia’s talent was beyond all compare.
lines.en: and Master Jia’s brilliance had no equal.

lines.py: kě lián yè bàn xū qián xí
lines.lit: A pity: at midnight he moved forward on his mat in vain —
lines.en: What a pity — at midnight he leaned in closer, for nothing:

lines.py: bù wèn cāng shēng wèn guǐ shén
lines.lit: he asked not about the common people, but about ghosts and spirits.
lines.en: he asked not about the people, but about ghosts and gods.

words.note: 生：古代对读书人的称呼。

words.en: the Xuanshi Hall of the Han palace

words.note: 贤：有才德的人，现代汉语“贤惠”“圣贤”。
调读 diào，现代汉语说“才华”“才气”。
古义多是“可惜”，今天多指“值得同情”。
古人席地而坐，听得入神就往前挪。

imagery.name: 宫阙
imagery.zh: 宣室是汉代未央宫的正殿，皇帝在这里召见贾谊，场面隆重。
imagery.en: Xuanshi was the main hall of the Han palace — a grand setting for the emperor to receive Jia Yi.
